full_story_part1.canonical_text:
A stone. Still a stone. Surely something will happen soon—no, it’s a stone. Nothing happens on the screen. That goes on for five minutes. But you, the viewer, can still get one thing done: cut someone else’s reward.

This sounds grim all of a sudden, but it’s about an online experiment with participants in the United States. They were randomly assigned to watch either a five-minute video of a stone, where nothing happened, or a video of a magician.

During that time, they had three choices: reduce another participant’s reward, increase it, or do nothing. They could change it by 10 cents at a time, up to a maximum of 50 cents. The stone on the screen stayed silent, while the viewers were handed “a little power.”

So, did boredom become fuel for meanness?

full_story_part2.text: Participants who were strongly inclined to enjoy seeing others suffer were more likely to reduce the other person's reward after watching the stone video than after watching the magician video. Among those with a weaker tendency, there was no clear difference. You might want to dismiss this by saying, So it really is a matter of personality. But there's more to the story. In the next experiment, participants were again randomly assigned to groups. But this time, there was no option to increase the reward. The only choice was to reduce it. This time, regardless of how strongly participants were inclined to enjoy seeing others suffer, those who watched the stone video were more likely to reduce another person's reward than those in the other conditions. Well, if we focus only on personality, we may miss something. Along with what kind of person someone is, there's also what they can do in that situation. We thought we were reading a profile of the person, but now we start noticing the stage setup, too.

full_story_part3.text: But it's too soon to jump to Add a button to increase rewards and bring world peace! The 2 were separate experiments. We can't say that the difference in choices alone caused the difference in results. We don't know that offering an increase option can prevent meanness. The experiment also dealt only with brief boredom and actions that reduced another person's reward. We can't apply its findings directly to everyday meanness or boredom that lasts a long time. Even so, our view of boring moments shifts a little. We can ask not only What mustn't I do? but also What else can I do instead? Before looking into someone's personality, look at the menu in front of us. The stone may not move for 5 minutes, but the question we ask shifts a little.

in_one_line.text: Stone-watchers were more likely to cut another person's reward—only those high in sadistic tendencies in one experiment, but people at every level in another. The findings suggest that the choices available in a situation may matter alongside personality. But these separate, brief experiments do not show that offering an increase option prevents meanness or that the findings apply to everyday life.
